# Draft:Biases in Juror Decision-Making

----
General Overview
The role of a juror is to listen to the evidence presented in trial, evaluate the facts, and make an impartial decision about whether the defendant is guilty (in a criminal case) or liable (in a civil case). Jurors are instructed to be impartial during this process, however, jurors may have implicit biases during this decision-making process. Implicit biases are unconscious predispositions that can automatically influence how people perceive and interact with others. A juror may intend on treating everyone equally but end up acting upon an implicit bias they have because these biases are typically present without the individual’s knowledge. This means that any implicit biases at play can impact verdicts, sentencing decisions, and overall fair treatment of anyone present during a trial.
Methods and Measurements
Biases in jury decision-making are typically measured using mock jury studies, in which people recruited for a study are asked to act as jurors in a simulated trial. That is, participants read, listen to, or watch trial materials (sometimes called “trial stimuli”) and then answer questions afterwards. The trial stimulus is often based on a real-world trial but has had the case facts altered to be more ambiguous and less recognizable. The trial information is typically presented in either a brief summary, a typed transcript of a trial, or through audio/video recordings. After reading, watching, or listening to the trial information, mock jurors answer a questionnaire that often contains questions about their chosen verdict, confidence in their verdict, and sentencing/punishment recommendations along with any other applicable questionnaires (for example, questionnaires that measure how credible jurors find a witness). Most jury research focuses on individual jurors, although some research does include the deliberation aspect. In this case, jurors choose their individual verdicts before deliberating with a group of other jurors. The group verdict is then recorded if the jury can come to an agreement. Then, individual jurors often still submit their individual verdicts again after deliberation along with answering any other applicable scales.
To specifically study biases in a jury decision-making process, the characteristics of the people in the trial stimuli are manipulated. For instance, the age, race, or gender of the defendant, witness, or attorney could be manipulated to examine whether jurors’ judgments change depending on the characteristics of the people presented to them. These characteristics can be manipulated through written description, using photographs, or by using videos of people with varying characteristics.
Age Biases
Defendants
According to U.S. federal court data, jurors and judges tend to be more lenient towards older defendants (60+ years old) than younger ones. As a result, younger defendants (under 60 years old) are more likely to be incarcerated than older defendants... Once a defendant is at the sentencing stage, meta-analysis research, which statistically combines results from multiple studies, indicated that defendant age did not affect sentencing length . This means that a defendant’s age may make a difference in whether they serve prison time, but not when determining their sentence length. Further mock-jury research found that there was leniency towards both older and younger defendants depending on the type of crime presented . When a murder case was presented, mock jurors assigned longer sentences to the 40-year-old defendant versus the 20 and 60-year-old defendants, and no age differences were found when the defendant was accused of theft. This is thought to be due to the serious nature of the murder (vs. theft) charge and because leniency tends to start once defendants reach at least 50 years old.
Witnesses
An eyewitness refers to someone who is present at the scene of the crime and may be called to testify in court about what they saw. In mock jury studies, child (vs. adult) witnesses are seen as less credible when testifying in court . This finding was extended across a five-study project looking at adult vs. child eyewitnesses, and the child witness led to fewer guilty verdicts than the adult witness . Mock jurors perceived children under the age of 10 years as having poorer recall than children over the age of 12, meaning that the age of the child may make a difference. According to a literature review, witnesses under the age of 18 were seen as more credible specifically when they provide smooth testimony with little hesitation .
Attorneys
There is currently no published research on how jurors may make decisions based upon the age of the attorney in the case.
Racial Biases
Defendants
Meta-analytic findings from 2005 concluded that there was a small effect of defendant race in both verdict and sentencing decisions to where people are harsher towards defendants of another race than their own . This racial bias was specifically pronounced amongst Black participants and in a sample of adults from the general population, compared to a sample of university students. Meta-analytic findings from 2024 show that mock jurors did not treat defendants differently based on their race for a variety of crimes, however, drug crimes were associated with a small racial bias effect harming both Black and Latino (vs. White) defendants . An additional meta-analysis from 2023 indicated finding no significant effect of race (comparing White defendants to defendants who are Black, Indigenous, or people of color) on legal decisions made by practitioners, investigators, and mock juries in cases involving forensic evidence .
Regarding the racial composition of the jury, a literature review from 1986 concluded that jurors made harsher decisions when (a) the defendant was of a different race than them and (b) the defendant and victim were not the same race . Differences were also seen specifically when defendant race was made salient in the stimuli. In this type of research, White mock jurors failed to show racial biases while Black mock jurors tended to show leniency towards defendants in their racial in-group . Racially diverse (vs. all-White) juries increased jurors’ cognitive depletion (a feeling of mental fatigue) while also increasing the number of case facts that jurors discussed during deliberation when the defendant was Black . Regardless of deliberation, mock jurors were less likely to find the Black (vs. White) defendant guilty.
As for cases involving the death penalty, there were no racial differences when a life sentence was the maximum sentence, but when the death penalty was the maximum sentence, mock jurors had an 80% conviction rate for Black defendants and a 55.1% conviction rate for White defendants . This aligns with research using photos of real defendants in Philadelphia who were facing the possibility of the death penalty . Participants rated how stereotypically Black each defendant appeared to be, and this information was used to determine that the defendants who were rated as more stereotypically Black were more likely to be sentenced to death (vs. life in prison) in real cases.
Research using U.S. federal court data showed that Hispanic defendants were more likely to be incarcerated than defendants of other races and that both Black and Hispanic defendants received the longest sentences compared with White defendants .
Witnesses
For eyewitnesses, race did not affect the verdict, but the Black (vs. White) eyewitness in a murder trial with a Black defendant was rated as more credible . An eyewitness is a person who directly observed a crime, and a character witness is someone who knows the defendant and testifies in court about the defendant’s moral character. When looking at Black and White character witnesses, the race of the character witness did not affect mock jurors’ verdicts . A co-conspirator informant witness is someone who participates in the execution of a crime along with the defendant and then provides the police with information and testimony against the defendant in hopes that they will receive a shorter sentence. The race (Black vs. White) of a co-conspirator informant witness also did not affect mock jurors’ verdicts in a drug case
Attorneys
Mock jurors perceived Mexican American defense attorneys as less competent when they were representing Mexican American (vs. European American) defendants, but the attorney’s race did not affect the verdict . When presented with a Black (vs. White) attorney, mock jurors were more likely to find the defendant guilty of murder . Additionally, a literature review argued that attorney race may interact with defendant race to produce differing juror judgments and called for more research on this topic .
Gender Biases
Defendants
Data from the U.S. Department of Justice revealed that there was a 565% increase in the rate of incarcerated women between 1980 and 2022 . Some analyses suggest that men are 74% more likely to be incarcerated than women for the same type of offense . A literature review focusing on cases of intimate partner violence, which involves abuse between current or former romantic partners, found that female defendants with male victims were treated more leniently than male defendants with female victims . A meta-analysis of mock jury studies aligned with this pattern and showed that women received significantly shorter sentences than men across crime types . Researchers suggest that this sentencing disparity may reflect cultural stereotypes that link masculinity with criminality  and associate men with more aggressive attitudes than women .
Witnesses
An expert witness is someone who testifies in court about a topic in which they are recognized by the court as an expert. A mock jury study found that female experts were perceived as more credible in fields where most professionals are women, whereas male experts were perceived as more credible in fields where most professionals are men . Other mock jury research revealed that people were more persuaded by a male (vs. female) expert witness when the testimony was complex, but that a female expert was more persuasive when the testimony lacked complexity . When mock jurors viewed an expert witness as either less likeable or less knowledgeable, they rated women more negatively than men in the same situation . A literature review suggested that the gender of an expert witness could influence the overall trial outcomes in civil cases, but the gender of an expert witness has little effect on outcomes in criminal cases .
Attorneys
In one study, mock jurors were more likely to acquit the defendant when they had a male (vs. female) attorney, and mock jurors showed a preference for attorneys who shared their own gender . When male attorneys expressed anger in court, participants viewed them more positively and cited their anger as a reason to hire them . When female attorneys expressed anger, participants viewed them more negatively and used their anger as a reason not to hire them. In a mock trial involving alleged rape, mock jurors rated a female (vs. male) prosecuting attorney as less competent and also perceived a female (vs. male) defense attorney as more competent. These perceptions of attorney competence, in turn, influenced jurors’ verdicts .
Intersectionality
Intersectionality is the idea that a person’s social identities, such as race, gender, and age, combine to shape their experiences and the advantages and disadvantages they face
In archival research on defendant race, gender, and age in Wisconsin, Black male defendants were the most likely to receive jail sentences, whereas Black female defendants were the least likely to receive jail sentences . In the same data, younger defendants generally had lower odds of incarceration, with the exception of Black male defendants, who were more likely to be incarcerated. Archival research in Pennsylvania revealed that young Black male and Hispanic male defendants received longer sentences than any other intersectional identities in the sample, and the shortest sentences were assigned to older defendants and young female defendants . Archival research using U.S. federal court data showed a similar pattern, finding that younger Hispanic male defendants were the most likely to be incarcerated, whereas young Black male defendants were the most likely to receive longer sentences . Overall, these archival studies indicated that the intersection of defendant age, gender, and race was associated with different sentencing outcomes, with several analyses finding particularly harsh outcomes for young Black male and younger Hispanic male defendants.
